# What this page covers

Two related questions about what the reads actually are, both answered on
**chr21 for all three timepoints** (2.29 M primary reads):

1. **Where do reads fall** — exon, intron, or intergenic, and by what rule?
2. **What exon structure does each read support** — which numbered exons it
   covers and how they are joined?

Scripts: `4.read_structure/` — `1.annotate_read_structure.py` does the
per-read CIGAR work, `2.summarise_structure.R` does the summary stats.
Outputs in `long_read_processed/read_structure/`.

The chr21 BAM excludes the rDNA array (chr21:8.2–8.6 Mb), which otherwise
contributes ~677 k rRNA carryover reads and would distort every fraction on
this page.

---

# Part 1 — exon / intron / intergenic

## The criterion

There is no canonical definition, so it has to be stated explicitly. For each
primary read:

1. **Parse the CIGAR into aligned reference blocks.** `M/=/X` extend a block;
   `N` (splice) and `D` break it; `I/S/H` consume no reference. This matters —
   97.8% of reads are soft-clipped, and counting clipped bases as aligned
   would corrupt every number below.
2. **Merge all annotated exons** into a flat interval set, and separately all
   genes. On chr21: 3,710 merged exon intervals, 328 gene intervals.
3. **Compute two fractions per read** — `f_exon` = aligned bases in exons /
   total aligned bases, and `f_gene` likewise.
4. **Classify:**

```
f_gene < 0.5                   -> intergenic
f_gene >= 0.5 and f_exon >= 0.5 -> exonic
f_gene >= 0.5 and f_exon < 0.5  -> intronic
```

The rule is **majority of aligned bases**, not "touches an exon". A read that
clips one exon and then runs 400 bp into an intron is intronic, which is the
behaviour you want for nuclear RNA.

## Results

| | 0 hr | 1 hr | 6 hr |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reads classified | 629,035 | 809,073 | 853,283 |
| **Exonic** | **29.00%** | **32.58%** | **32.05%** |
| **Intronic** | **64.82%** | **61.60%** | **62.65%** |
| Intergenic | 6.18% | 5.82% | 5.30% |
| Spliced (CIGAR `N`) | 19.43% | 20.61% | 20.49% |

The spliced fractions land within 0.6 pp of the genome-wide per-cell numbers
(19.45 / 20.17 / 19.87), so chr21 behaves as a fair sample of the whole.

## How much the rule changes the answer

Same reads, three rules, 0 hr:

| Rule | Exonic | Intronic |
|---|---|---|
| Permissive — *any* exon overlap | 35.50% | 58.55% |
| **Majority — ≥50% of bases** | **29.00%** | **64.82%** |
| Strict — ≥90% / ≤10% | 26.58% | 59.89% (+7.35% mixed) |

Exonic swings between 26.6% and 35.5% on the choice of rule alone. **Any single
"% exonic" figure is meaningless without the criterion attached.**

## Introns dominate because they are large, not because enrichment failed

On chr21 exons are only **8.9% of genic sequence** (1.86 Mb of 21.0 Mb). If
reads landed uniformly across genes, 8.9% of genic bases would be exonic.
Observed:

| | Exonic share of genic bases | Enrichment over uniform |
|---|---|---|
| 0 hr | 32.6% | **3.7×** |
| 1 hr | 35.8% | 4.0× |
| 6 hr | 35.5% | 4.0× |

So the library *is* strongly exon-enriched, ~4×, and introns still dominate the
read count simply because there is ~11× more intronic sequence. This is a
normal single-*nucleus* library, not a failed one.

## Reconciling with the scNanoGPS slides

The slides report **68.40% intronic / 11.62% exonic**. Our intronic (64.8%) is
close; our exonic (29.0%) is not.

That gap is the criterion, not an error in either number. Their "exonic" is
almost certainly **transcript compatibility** — the read must be consistent
with an annotated exon structure — which is much stricter than base overlap.
Consistency check: only **19.43% of reads are spliced at all**, so a rule
requiring validated junction structure caps out near 19%, and 11.62% sits
plausibly below that.

Two caveats on our numbers: we used the **IsoQuant extended** annotation, which
adds 22,490 novel transcripts and therefore inflates "exonic" relative to plain
GENCODE; and this is chr21 with the rDNA array removed.

# Part 2 — per-read exon structure

## Exon numbering

Per-transcript numbering is ambiguous — the same physical exon is #3 in one
isoform and #5 in another. Instead we flatten: the **union of all exons of all
transcripts of a gene, merged, numbered 1..N in 5'→3' order** (reversed on the
minus strand). This matches isoLASER's exonic-part model, so the two analyses
are directly comparable.

## Notation

```
E1-E2-E3   consecutive exons joined by splice junctions
E1-E3      E2 bypassed
E1=E2      contiguous alignment through the intron (retention, >=50% covered)
E4         single exon, no junction
INTRONIC   assigned to a gene but no exon covered (>=10 bp to "cover")
INTERGENIC not assignable to a gene
```

## An artifact that had to be fixed first

The first pass gave `SKIP` (46,485 reads) **greater than** `CONSECUTIVE`
(40,321), and the most common pattern on the chromosome was `SON E1-E2-E4`.
That is not exon skipping. The union numbering inserts rare isoform-specific
exons into the sequence:

| Gene | "Skipped" exon | Size | Transcript support |
|---|---|---|---|
| SON | E3 | 39 bp | 1 / 23 |
| ATP5PF | E3 | 43 bp | 1 / 8 |
| SOD1 | E3 | 186 bp | 1 / 5 |

`SON E1-E2-E4` is the **canonical** structure — it only looks like skipping
because a 1-of-23 exon occupies position 3.

Fix: skip-calling is now transcript-aware. A bypassed exon must be present in
**≥2 transcripts** to count as skipping; otherwise the read is `SKIP_MINOR`.
After the fix `SKIP` is 2.51% and sits below `CONSECUTIVE` at 6.41%.

> This bias is inherited by **any** analysis that flattens the IsoQuant
> extended annotation — including how we read isoLASER's exonic parts.

## Read classes

Percent of reads, chr21:

| Class | 0 hr | 1 hr | 6 hr |
|---|---|---|---|
| INTRONIC | 59.96 | 56.25 | 56.98 |
| SINGLE_EXON | 19.33 | 21.88 | 21.86 |
| CONSECUTIVE | 6.41 | 7.25 | 7.03 |
| INTERGENIC | 6.18 | 5.83 | 5.31 |
| SKIP_MINOR | 4.88 | 5.16 | 5.02 |
| **SKIP** | **2.51** | **2.90** | **3.01** |
| RETAINED | 0.58 | 0.62 | 0.67 |
| MIXED | 0.14 | 0.12 | 0.13 |

The number that matters: **only 9.5% of reads carry more than one exon**
(CONSECUTIVE + SKIP + SKIP_MINOR + RETAINED + MIXED at 0 hr). That is the
entire population capable of informing on splicing.

## Junction novelty

Among spliced reads only:

| | 0 hr | 1 hr | 6 hr |
|---|---|---|---|
| All junctions annotated | 63.82 | 68.36 | 67.14 |
| Some novel | 8.76 | 7.54 | 7.89 |
| **All novel** | **27.41** | **24.11** | **24.98** |

**These novel rates are not yet trustworthy** — see the caveats section.

## Skipping and retention

Among multi-exon reads:

| | 0 hr | 1 hr | 6 hr |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supported skip | 17.35% | 18.15% | 19.10% |
| Minor-exon bypass only | 34.16% | 32.46% | 31.92% |
| ≥1 retained intron | 5.01% | 4.61% | 5.01% |

## Most structurally diverse genes

0 hr, counting patterns with ≥20 reads:

| Gene | Distinct patterns | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| TTC3 | 122 | 17,022 |
| APP | 77 | 18,723 |
| BRWD1 | 35 | 4,400 |
| LTN1 | 33 | 1,909 |
| GRIK1 | 31 | 5,837 |
| NCAM2 | 30 | 3,095 |
| DSCAM | 29 | 2,274 |

Top genuine skipping events at 0 hr:

| Gene | Pattern | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| NDUFV3 | E4-E5-E8 | 886 |
| GET1 | E3-E6-E7-E8-E9 | 768 |
| PTTG1IP | E1-E6-E8-E9-E10 | 717 |
| ATP5PF | E1-E4-E5-E6 | 607 |
| PIGP | E1-E3-E4-E5 | 531 |
| MRPS6 | E2-E6-E7 | 312 |
| BACH1 | E5-E11-E12 | 259 |

## The 3' bias, measured directly

Every top single-exon pattern is a **terminal** exon — APP E27, COL6A1 E35,
TTC3 E54, BRWD1 E42. Quantified over single-exon reads in genes with ≥5 exons
(n = 110,412, 0 hr):

| Position along gene (5'→3') | Share of reads |
|---|---|
| first 20% | 15.6% |
| 20–40% | 10.1% |
| 40–60% | 7.4% |
| 60–80% | 13.3% |
| **last 20%** | **53.6%** |

**41.7% cover the final exon; 3.2% cover the first — a 13× ratio.**

This is the 10x 3' chemistry appearing directly in the structure annotation,
and it is the cleanest statement of the dataset's core limitation: reads sample
the 3' end, so splicing information is concentrated at the 3' end of genes and
there is little power over 5' events.

---

# Caveats

**The 27% all-novel junction rate is too high to be discovery.** The IsoQuant
extended annotation already contains 22,490 novel transcripts, so genuinely
unannotated junctions should be rarer than this. The likely cause is the 5 bp
matching tolerance against ~1.1% ONT base error — minimap2 placing junctions a
few bases off the true site. Before any of these are read as novel splicing the
tolerance needs calibrating against splice-site motifs (GT-AG). **The
novel-junction numbers should not be reported yet.**

**The timepoint trends are small and donor-pooled.** Exonic rises
29.00 → 32.58 → 32.05%, intronic falls 64.82 → 61.60 → 62.65%, and supported
skipping rises 17.35 → 19.10%. The direction is consistent with
post-stimulation transcript maturation, and 0 hr separates from both stimulated
points (~3 pp) while 1 hr and 6 hr differ from each other by ~0.5 pp. But
donors are pooled and this is one chromosome — library-level differences in
nuclear/cytoplasmic capture would produce the same pattern.

It is worth noting that this trend is **independent of the barcode metadata**,
so it serves as a weak cross-check on the timepoint labels alongside the
planned IEG measurement.

**Annotation choice matters.** All of the above uses the IsoQuant extended
annotation. A plain GENCODE run would give fewer flattened exons, fewer
`SKIP_MINOR` calls, and a lower exonic fraction.

# What this implies for the two aims

**Aim 1 (splicing changes during the response).** With ~60% of reads intronic
and only 9.5% carrying multiple exons, isoform-level quantification discards
most of the data. Junction-level counting and intron retention use what is
actually present. Intron retention in particular is well matched to nuclear RNA
and is measured per molecule by long reads.

**Aim 2 (genetic variants associated with splicing).** The 3' bias localises
where power exists: a heterozygous SNP and a splicing event must fall on the
same read, and both are concentrated in terminal exons. This is consistent with
the 98.5% untestable rate seen in the
[chr21 isoLASER run](isolaser_per_donor.html).

# Next steps

* Run this per **donor × timepoint** (12 groups) so the trends can be tested
  within donors rather than on pooled data.
* Calibrate the junction-matching tolerance against GT-AG motifs before
  reporting anything about novel junctions.
* Extend genome-wide once the full GRCh38 FASTA is in place.
